title: analogWrite
summary: To output a PWM signal in Arduino code, we use the analogWrite() function!

steps.title: analogWrite

quickCheck.question: What symbol on the Arduino Uno printed silkscreen marks digital pins that support PWM output?
quickCheck.explanation: Pins marked with a tilde (~) such as 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, and 11 support hardware PWM output.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Look at the digital pin headers on your Arduino board: the wavy line ~ marks PWM pins.

quickCheck.question: In the Arduino analogWrite(pin, value) command, what value produces full 100% brightness?
quickCheck.explanation: analogWrite uses an 8-bit scale from 0 (OFF) to 255 (maximum 100% duty cycle).
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Arduino PWM operates on an 8-bit scale: 0 is completely off, and 255 is maximum power.

steps.title: The analogWrite() Function Range (0 to 255)
steps.markdownContent:
### The 8-Bit Number Range
In Arduino C++, the command to output PWM is .

Even though it has "analog" in the name, it actually outputs a digital PWM square wave!

The  parameter is an **8-bit integer** ranging from **0 to 255**:
-  -> 0% duty cycle (OFF)
-  -> 25% duty cycle
-  -> 50% duty cycle
-  -> 100% duty cycle (Full brightness)

questions.question: What range of values does analogWrite() accept?
questions.explanation: Arduino Uno uses 8-bit PWM timers, giving 256 discrete levels (0 to 255)!

questions.question: What duty cycle does analogWrite(pin, 127) produce approximately?
questions.explanation: 127 is roughly half of 255, producing a 50% duty cycle!
